extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, math enthusiasts, authors/educators interested in proof aesthetics and expository selection
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and composing mathematical proofs for elegance/beauty (as in selections for Aigner & Ziegler's 'Proofs from THE BOOK'), emphasizing brevity, clarity, a single special idea, unexpected connections, and reader-relative comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: "A proof that eats more than 10 pages cannot be a proof for our book."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short proofs are preferred; excessive length disqualifies a proof for the book. Brevity is one of the necessary components of 'beauty' (see composite principle). No explicit page-count rule beyond the quoted threshold, but concision and economy of presentation are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof must be understandable to readers, not just technically correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understandability to the intended audience is required — clear explanation, transparent logical flow, and exposition that communicates the idea, not merely formal correctness. Clarity interacts with reader knowledge (see reader-dependent beauty).

rubrics_metrics.name: A Special Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should contain an innovative or surprising concept; mere correctness is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer proofs organized around a single unifying or striking idea — an insight or trick that illuminates why the result holds. The presence of such an idea distinguishes beautiful proofs from routine verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected Connections
rubrics_metrics.description: "Connect[s] things that usually one wouldn't think of as having any connection."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs that reveal relationships between disparate areas or concepts are favored. Example given: Lovász's use of topology to solve a graph-theory problem (Kneser conjecture). Such cross-field uses of methods increase perceived beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-Dependent Beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whether the proof is understandable and beautiful depends not only on the proof but also on the reader: What do you know?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation must account for the audience's background — what is elegant to one reader may be opaque to another. Selection/exposition should consider reader knowledge and pedagogical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple Proofs Are Valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple proofs of the same theorem reveal different truths and let mathematicians "understand the situation beyond the original basic theorem."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage collecting and presenting different proofs: alternative approaches can illuminate different aspects of a theorem and are collectively important for understanding. This principle supports inclusion of varied proofs rather than privileging a single canonical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise of Tool / Use of Unexpected Techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a tool or area (e.g., topology) in an unexpected domain (e.g., graph theory) is a source of aesthetic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deployment of methods from outside the usual toolkit for a problem is specifically praised as adding surprise and insight. Such examples serve as models for what counts as an 'unexpected connection.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitability versus Wonder (Two Registers of Beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proofs feel inevitable after discovery; others retain mystery. Both registers are admissible as beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both styles — proofs that seem 'natural/inevitable' and those that preserve a sense of wonder or mystery — are acceptable forms of aesthetic value. Do not require a proof to conform to one register exclusively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence Through Ugliness (Value of Ugly Proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ugly proofs serve a purpose: establishing truth first, enabling later elegant simplifications. The first proof need not be beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the pragmatic role of messy or technical proofs in establishing results; such proofs are valuable historically and scientifically and can be precursors to later elegant treatments. Lack of immediate beauty does not invalidate usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as a Composite Criterion (All Five Necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty decomposes into: brevity + clarity + a single special idea + unexpected connection + reader-relative comprehension. All five are necessary; no one alone suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat aesthetic quality as the conjunction of multiple dimensions rather than any single attribute. When judging or selecting proofs, require a balance of these components: brevity, clarity, a special conceptual idea, an unexpected connection, and fit to the reader. Omitting any one component undermines the claim of 'perfect' or 'Book' proof status.
